mainEntity.name: What are the types of variables in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java has three types of variables based on where they are declared: (1) Local variables — declared inside a method, constructor, or block. They exist only within that scope and must be initialized before use. No default value. (2) Instance variables (non-static fields) — declared inside a class but outside any method. Each object gets its own copy. They have default values (0, false, null). (3) Static variables (class variables) — declared with the static keyword inside a class but outside methods. Shared across all instances of the class. Also have default values.

mainEntity.name: What is the var keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: var is a reserved type name introduced in Java 10 for local variable type inference. Instead of writing the full type, you write var and the compiler infers the type from the right-hand side: var name = 'Alice'; — compiler infers String. var list = new ArrayList<String>(); — compiler infers ArrayList<String>. var can only be used for local variables with an initializer — not for fields, method parameters, return types, or catch parameters (except catch from Java 10). var is still statically typed — the type is fixed at compile time, not at runtime. It improves readability for long generic types.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between local, instance, and static variables in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Local variable: declared inside a method/block, no default value (must initialize before use), stored on stack, scope limited to the declaring block, not accessible with this or class name. Instance variable: declared in class body outside methods, has default value (0/false/null), stored on heap with the object, each object has its own copy, accessed via this.fieldName or object.fieldName. Static variable: declared with static keyword in class body, has default value, stored in method area (shared memory), one copy shared by all objects, accessed via ClassName.fieldName.

mainEntity.name: What are the naming conventions for variables in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java variable naming follows camelCase convention: start with a lowercase letter, capitalize each subsequent word — firstName, totalAmount, isActive. Rules: must start with a letter, underscore (_), or dollar sign ($) — not a digit. Cannot be a Java keyword (int, class, static, etc.). Case-sensitive — count and Count are different variables. Constants (static final) use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — MAX_SIZE, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, PI. Avoid single-letter names except for loop counters (i, j, k) and simple lambdas. Use meaningful, descriptive names — customerAge not ca, invoiceTotal not t.

mainEntity.name: What is a final variable in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A final variable in Java can only be assigned once — after the first assignment, its value cannot be changed. For primitives, final means the value is constant. For objects, final means the reference cannot be reassigned, but the object's internal state can still be modified. Local final variables must be initialized before use. Instance final variables must be initialized either at declaration or in every constructor. Static final variables (constants) must be initialized at declaration or in a static block. Convention: name static final constants in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — public static final double PI = 3.14159;

articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java Variables — what they are, three types (local, instance, static), data types, default values, var keyword, final variables, constants, naming conventions, scope and lifetime, variable shadowing, and real-world production code examples.

sections.title: What is a Variable in Java?

blocks.text: A variable is a named container that holds a value in memory. When you declare a variable in Java, the JVM reserves a memory location, gives it a name, and associates a data type with it. The data type determines what kind of value the variable can hold — a whole number, a decimal, a single character, a true/false flag, or a reference to an object.

Every variable in Java has three essential components: (1) Type — what kind of data it stores (int, String, double, etc.). (2) Name — the identifier used to access it (age, userName, totalPrice). (3) Value — the actual data stored (25, "Alice", 99.99). Java is a statically typed language — every variable's type is fixed at compile time and cannot change at runtime.

blocks.label: VariableBasics.java
lines: boolean isActive = true;        // true or false
String name = "Priya";         // text (String is a class, not primitive)
int score;           // Declared but not yet initialized
// System.out.println(score); // ❌ Compile error: variable not initialized
score = 95;          // Now initialized — safe to use
count = 2;   // Reassigned — old value 1 is gone

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Variable at a Glance
blocks.text: Declaration: dataType variableName; — reserves memory. Initialization: variableName = value; — stores a value. Declaration + Initialization: dataType variableName = value; — both at once. Java is statically typed — type is fixed at compile time. Local variables must be explicitly initialized before use — no default. Instance and static variables get default values automatically (0, false, null). Variable names are case-sensitive: age and Age are different variables.

sections.title: Types of Variables in Java

blocks.text: Java classifies variables into three types based on where they are declared — which determines their scope (where they can be accessed), lifetime (how long they exist in memory), and default values (what value they hold before explicit assignment).

items.title: Local Variables
items.text: Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Scope is limited to that block — cannot be accessed from outside. No default value — must be initialized before use or the compiler will refuse to compile. Stored on the stack. Created when the method is called, destroyed when the method returns. Cannot have access modifiers (public, private, etc.).

items.title: Instance Variables (Non-static Fields)
items.text: Declared inside a class body but outside any method, without the static keyword. Each object (instance) of the class gets its own separate copy. Have default values — 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for object references. Stored on the heap along with the object. Lifetime matches the object — created when object is created, destroyed when object is garbage collected. Can have access modifiers.

items.title: Static Variables (Class Variables)
items.text: Declared inside a class body with the static keyword, outside any method. Only one copy exists for the entire class — shared across all instances. Have default values like instance variables. Stored in the method area (class memory). Lifetime matches the class — loaded when class is loaded, destroyed when JVM shuts down or class is unloaded. Accessed via ClassName.variableName. Can have access modifiers.

sections.title: Local Variables — Method-Level Variables

blocks.text: Local variables are declared inside a method, constructor, block (if, for, while, try), or lambda. They are the most commonly used variables in Java and have the tightest scope — they exist only within the block they are declared in. The compiler does not assign default values to local variables — using an uninitialized local variable is a compile-time error.

blocks.label: LocalVariables.java
lines: }  // quantity, unitPrice, total are destroyed here
int inner = 20;  // Local to this if-block only
// System.out.println(inner);  // ❌ Compile error: inner out of scope
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {  // i is local to the for loop
// System.out.println(i);  // ❌ Compile error: i out of scope
int x;  // Declared but not initialized
// System.out.println(x);  // ❌ Compile error: variable x not initialized
// ❌ Compile error — compiler cannot guarantee result was initialized
// (even though condition is always true — compiler doesn't evaluate)
// ✅ Fix: initialize in all branches or give default

blocks.title: ⚠️ Local Variables Have No Default Value
blocks.text: Unlike instance and static variables, local variables are NOT automatically initialized. Using an uninitialized local variable is a compile-time error — the compiler will refuse to compile: 'variable x might not have been initialized'. This is a safety feature — it prevents accidental use of garbage values. Always initialize local variables either at declaration (int count = 0;) or before their first use. The compiler performs definite assignment analysis — it checks that the variable is initialized on every possible code path before use.

sections.title: Instance Variables — Object-Level Fields

blocks.text: Instance variables (also called fields or non-static fields) are declared inside a class body but outside any method or block, without the static keyword. They represent the state of an object — each object created from the class gets its own private copy of every instance variable. Changes to one object's instance variable do not affect another object's copy.

blocks.label: InstanceVariables.java
lines: // ── Instance variables — each Student object gets its own copy ───────
// ── Constructor — sets instance variables at creation ────────────────
public Student(String name, int age, double gpa) {
this.name = name;  // 'this' distinguishes instance var from param
this.isEnrolled = true;  // Default for new students
// ── Each object has its OWN copy of instance variables ───────────
// Name: Priya | Age: 20 | GPA: 8.5 | Enrolled: true
// Name: Rahul | Age: 22 | GPA: 7.8 | Enrolled: true
// ── Changing s1's variable does NOT affect s2 ────────────────────
// int → 0, double → 0.0, boolean → false, String → null

sections.title: Static Variables — Class-Level Shared Variables

blocks.text: Static variables (also called class variables) are declared with the static keyword inside a class body, outside any method. There is only one copy of a static variable — shared by all instances of the class. If one object changes a static variable, the change is visible to all other objects. Static variables are ideal for data that belongs to the class as a whole, not to individual objects — such as counters, configuration constants, and shared state.

blocks.label: StaticVariables.java
lines: // ── Static variable — ONE copy shared by ALL BankAccount objects ─────
static int totalAccounts = 0;         // Tracks how many accounts exist
static double interestRate = 6.5;     // Same rate for all accounts
// ── Instance variables — each account has its own ────────────────────
this.accountNumber = totalAccounts; // Unique number per account
// ── Static variable accessed via class name (preferred) ───────────
// ── Also accessible via instance (not recommended — misleading) ───
// ── Changing static variable affects ALL instances ────────────────
BankAccount.interestRate = 7.0;  // Rate change for all accounts

blocks.title: 💡 Access Static Variables via Class Name
blocks.text: Always access static variables using the class name — BankAccount.totalAccounts — not via an instance reference — acc1.totalAccounts. Both compile and work, but the class-name syntax makes it immediately clear that the variable is shared (static), not object-specific. Code reviewers and tools like IntelliJ and SonarLint flag instance-style access to static members as a warning. This is especially important when reading code — seeing ClassName.field instantly signals 'this is shared state'.

sections.title: Data Types for Variables

blocks.text: Every Java variable must have a declared type. Java has two categories of data types: primitive types — the 8 built-in value types — and reference types — objects, arrays, and interfaces. The type determines what values the variable can hold and how much memory it occupies.

blocks.label: DataTypes.java
lines: long   l  = 9_000_000_000L; // 64-bit | very large numbers (suffix L)
float  f  = 3.14f;         // 32-bit | 7 decimal digits precision (suffix f)
char   c2 = 65;            // Also 'A' — stored as Unicode code point
boolean flag = true;       // true or false only

sections.title: Default Values of Variables

blocks.text: Java automatically assigns default values to instance variables and static variables when they are declared without initialization. Local variables do NOT get default values — using them before initialization causes a compile-time error. Understanding default values is important because uninitialized instance fields quietly hold these defaults — which can lead to subtle bugs if you forget to set them in a constructor.

blocks.label: DefaultValues.java
lines: // ── Instance variables — get default values automatically ────────────

blocks.title: 📌 Default Value Summary
blocks.text: byte, short, int, long → 0. float → 0.0f. double → 0.0. char → '\u0000' (null character, not '0'). boolean → false. Any object reference (String, arrays, custom classes) → null. These defaults apply to instance variables and static variables only. Local variables have NO default — compiler enforces initialization. Relying silently on default null for String or object fields is a common source of NullPointerException bugs — always initialize fields explicitly in constructors.

sections.title: var Keyword — Local Variable Type Inference (Java 10+)

blocks.text: Java 10 introduced local variable type inference via the var keyword. Instead of writing the explicit type, you write var and the compiler infers the type from the right-hand side expression. var is not a dynamic type — the variable is still statically typed at compile time, the type is just written by the compiler instead of you. This reduces verbosity for long generic types while keeping full type safety.

blocks.label: VarKeyword.java
lines: // ── var shines with long generic types ───────────────────────────
HashMap<String, List<Integer>> oldStyle = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {  // i is int
// ── RESTRICTIONS — where var CANNOT be used ──────────────────────
// var x;  // Compile error: cannot infer type
// var obj = null;  // Compile error: cannot infer type from null
// ❌ var is LOCAL ONLY — not for fields or method params
// ❌ var NOT allowed as field type
// ❌ var NOT allowed as method parameter
// ❌ var NOT allowed as return type

blocks.title: 💡 var — When to Use and When Not to
blocks.text: USE var when: the type is obvious from the right-hand side (var name = 'Alice'; — clearly String), the type name is long and generic (var map = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();), in for-each loops (for (var item : list)), with stream intermediate variables. AVOID var when: the right-hand side doesn't clearly communicate the type (var result = process(); — what type is result?), it reduces readability for team members, for primitive literals where the type is already short (int x = 0; is clearer than var x = 0;). var is about reducing noise — not about hiding types.

sections.title: final Variables & Constants

blocks.text: The final keyword applied to a variable means it can be assigned only once. After the first assignment, any attempt to reassign it causes a compile-time error. For primitive final variables, the value itself is constant. For reference final variables, the reference is fixed — you cannot point it to a different object — but the object's internal state can still be modified. Constants in Java are declared as public static final and named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

blocks.label: FinalVariables.java
lines: // ── Constants — public static final — class-level constants ──────────
public static final String APP_NAME    = "Tech Sustainify";
// ── Final instance variable — must be set in constructor ──────────────
this.username = username;  // Assigned once in constructor
// MAX_SCORE = 200;  // ❌ Compile error: cannot assign to final
// ── Final reference — REFERENCE is fixed, object state is not ────
// cities = new ArrayList<>(); // ❌ Compile error: cannot reassign final ref

blocks.title: 📌 final vs Constants — Quick Rules
blocks.text: final local variable: cannot be reassigned after first assignment. final instance variable: must be initialized at declaration or in every constructor. final static variable (constant): must be initialized at declaration or in a static block. Naming: local final → camelCase (final int maxScore = 100). Class-level constant → UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (public static final int MAX_SIZE = 50). final reference: the reference is fixed, not the object — you can call mutating methods on a final object reference. For truly immutable objects, the class itself must be immutable (like String).

sections.title: Naming Conventions — Writing Readable Java Variable Names

blocks.text: Java has well-established naming conventions that every professional developer follows. These are not enforced by the compiler — they are community standards that make code readable, maintainable, and consistent across teams and projects. Following them signals professionalism and makes code reviews much smoother.

items.title: Variables & Parameters — camelCase
items.text: Start with a lowercase letter. Capitalize the first letter of each subsequent word. Examples: firstName, totalAmount, isActive, customerAge, invoiceTotal, maxRetryCount. Avoid abbreviations unless universally understood (url, id, html are fine; cstmr for customer is not). Single-letter names are only acceptable for loop counters (i, j, k) and short lambda parameters.

items.title: Constants — UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
items.text: All static final variables use all uppercase letters with words separated by underscores. Examples: MAX_SIZE, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, PI, MAX_RETRY_COUNT, BASE_URL, APP_VERSION. This naming instantly signals to any reader that the value is constant and shared — a visual contract. Never use camelCase for constants.

items.title: Boolean Variables — is / has / can Prefix
items.text: Boolean variables and methods should read as yes/no questions. Use prefixes: isActive, isEnrolled, hasPermission, canEdit, isEmpty, wasDeleted. This makes conditions read naturally: if (isActive), if (hasPermission). Avoid names like active or enrolled alone for booleans — they are ambiguous.

items.title: Valid Identifier Rules
items.text: Must start with a letter (a-z, A-Z), underscore (_), or dollar sign ($). Cannot start with a digit. Cannot be a Java keyword (int, class, return, static, etc.). Can contain letters, digits, underscores, dollar signs. Case-sensitive — count and Count are different. Length limit is effectively unlimited. Avoid $ and _ as prefixes in application code — reserved for generated/framework code conventions.

blocks.label: NamingConventions.java — Good vs Bad
lines: private int    a;             // ❌ Meaningless single letter (not a loop)
private double TotalAmount;   // ❌ Starts with uppercase (looks like class)
private boolean active;       // ❌ Ambiguous for boolean — use isActive
private int    max_retries;   // ❌ snake_case for variable (use camelCase)
private static final int maxSize = 100;    // ❌ Should be MAX_SIZE
private static final double pi = 3.14;    // ❌ Should be PI
// ── ✅ Valid but unusual identifiers (avoid in practice) ──────────────
int _count = 0;     // Valid but avoid leading underscore
int $temp  = 0;     // Valid but $ is for generated code
int i2     = 0;     // Valid — digit not at start
// int my var = 0;   // ❌ Space not allowed

sections.title: Scope & Lifetime of Variables

blocks.text: Scope defines where in the code a variable can be accessed. Lifetime defines how long the variable exists in memory. These two concepts are closely related but distinct — a variable's scope is determined by where it's declared in the source code, while its lifetime is a runtime concept tied to execution context and garbage collection.

blocks.label: ScopeAndLifetime.java
lines: // ── Class scope — accessible anywhere in this class ──────────────────
static int classVar = 100;       // Static: lives as long as the class
int instanceVar = 200;            // Instance: lives as long as the object
// ── Method scope — accessible only in this method ────────────────
// ── Block scope — only inside this if block ──────────────────
// System.out.println(blockVar); // ❌ blockVar out of scope here
// ── Loop scope — i exists only within the loop ───────────────
int loopBody = i * 10;  // New variable each iteration

sections.title: Variable Shadowing — When Inner Hides Outer

blocks.text: Variable shadowing occurs when a variable declared in an inner scope has the same name as a variable in an outer scope. The inner variable shadows (hides) the outer one within its scope. In Java, a local variable can shadow an instance variable — the local variable takes precedence inside the method. The this keyword is used to explicitly refer to the instance variable when both exist in scope.

blocks.label: VariableShadowing.java
lines: // ── Most common shadowing: constructor/method parameter vs field ─────
this.name = name;  // Assigns parameter value to instance field
// ❌ Cannot re-declare x inside — Java does not allow local-to-local
// int x = 20;  // Compile error: variable x already defined
// Note: Java prevents shadowing LOCAL with another LOCAL in same method
// But a local CAN shadow an INSTANCE variable (shown above)

blocks.title: ⚠️ Shadowing Rules in Java
blocks.text: A local variable CAN shadow an instance variable (same name allowed — use this.varName to access the instance one). A local variable CANNOT shadow another local variable in the same method scope — compiler error: 'variable already defined'. In a static method, there is no this — use ClassName.staticVar to access the static field when shadowed. Shadowing is most commonly seen (and intentionally used) in constructors and setters where the parameter name matches the field name: this.name = name is the idiomatic pattern.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Variable Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These are the most common variable-related mistakes in Java — frequently seen in beginner code and surprisingly also in experienced developer codebases under time pressure.

blocks.label: VariableMistakes.java
lines: // System.out.println(score);  // Compile error: variable score not initialized
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: int overflow — result wraps around silently
int overflow = max + 1;       // -2147483648 — silent wrap, no exception!
// ✅ Fix: use long for large numbers
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Integer division truncates — losing decimal part
double result = a / b;         // 3.0 — NOT 3.5! Division done as int
// ✅ Fix: cast one operand to double
// if (x = 10) { }  // Compile error: int cannot be used as boolean
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: float precision — unexpected decimal behavior
// ✅ Use double for better precision; use BigDecimal for exact money calculations
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Accessing static variable via instance — misleading
// acc.interestRate = 7.0;  // Misleads readers — looks like instance field
System.out.println((char)(c + 1)); // 'B' — must cast back to char
// ❌ MISTAKE 8: Forgetting L suffix for large long literals
// long bigNum = 10000000000;    // Compile error: int literal out of range
long bigNum = 10_000_000_000L;   // ✅ Correct with L suffix
// ❌ MISTAKE 9: Comparing strings with == instead of .equals()

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns represent common misuses of variables in professional Java code. Each one makes code harder to read, maintain, or reason about.

items.title: Reusing the Same Variable for Different Purposes
items.text: Using one variable to hold different meanings at different points in a method — int temp = calculateTax(); then later temp = processRefund(); — makes the code impossible to understand. Declare a new variable with a meaningful name for each distinct value. Variable declarations are cheap; the confusion from reuse is expensive. This is sometimes called 'variable recycling' and it is universally rejected in code reviews.

items.title: Declaring All Variables at the Top of a Method
items.text: A legacy style from older languages: declaring all local variables at the top of a method regardless of where they are used. Modern Java practice is to declare variables as close as possible to their first use — this keeps scope tight, makes the code easier to follow, and reduces the chance of accidental misuse. The compiler optimizes either way, so there is no performance reason to declare early.

items.title: Using Magic Numbers Instead of Named Constants
items.text: Writing if (retries > 3) or price * 1.18 instead of named constants MAX_RETRIES and GST_RATE. Magic numbers have no self-documenting meaning — readers must guess what 3 or 1.18 means. When the value changes, you must hunt down every occurrence. Fix: declare public static final constants with descriptive names. The constant is written once, read everywhere, and changed in one place.

items.title: Overly Wide Scope — Variables Declared Too Early
items.text: Declaring a variable outside a loop when it is only needed inside, or as an instance variable when it should be local. Wide scope increases the chance of accidental modification, makes thread-safety harder, and confuses readers about the variable's purpose. The principle of least scope: declare a variable in the smallest scope that correctly satisfies its use. If a variable is only needed inside an if-block, declare it inside the if-block.

items.title: Not Making Variables final When They Should Be
items.text: Failing to mark local variables and method parameters as final when they are never reassigned. Making variables final communicates intent ('this value will not change'), prevents accidental reassignment bugs, and enables better compiler/JIT optimization. In modern Java codebases, many teams enforce that all variables that are never reassigned must be declared final. This is trivially enforced with tools like Checkstyle or SpotBugs.

items.title: Meaningless or Cryptic Variable Names
items.text: Names like d, tmp, x1, x2, val, data, obj, or result without context. These force every reader to mentally trace the code to understand what the variable holds. Meaningful names act as inline documentation: customerDiscountAmount explains itself; cda does not. The extra characters cost nothing at runtime — the compiler optimizes away names. Invest in names — they are the most read part of any codebase.

sections.title: Java Variables Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java developer interviews at all levels — from campus placements to senior engineer rounds. Variable types, scope, and the var keyword are frequently tested topics.

items.q: Q1. What are the types of variables in Java? Explain each.
items.a: Java has three types of variables: (1) Local variables — declared inside methods, constructors, or blocks. No default value — must be initialized before use. Scope limited to the declaring block. Stored on the stack. (2) Instance variables — declared inside a class body but outside methods, without static. Each object has its own copy. Default values assigned automatically (0, false, null). Stored on the heap. Scope is the entire class. (3) Static variables — declared with the static keyword in the class body. Only one copy shared across all instances. Default values assigned. Stored in method area. Accessed via ClassName.variableName.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between instance variable and local variable?
items.a: Instance variable: declared in class body outside methods. Belongs to an object — each instance has its own copy. Has a default value (0/false/null). Accessible throughout the class via this.varName. Lifetime matches the object. Can have access modifiers. Local variable: declared inside a method or block. Belongs to that method call. No default value — compile error if used uninitialized. Accessible only within the declaring block. Lifetime matches the method execution. Cannot have access modifiers. Key test: an instance variable uninitialized in a constructor will silently hold its default value (null for String — potential NPE later); a local variable uninitialized is a compile-time error.

items.q: Q3. What is a static variable? When should you use it?
items.a: A static variable (class variable) is declared with the static keyword inside a class but outside methods. There is only ONE copy shared by all instances of the class. It is created when the class is loaded and destroyed when the JVM exits. Use static variables for: shared counters (total objects created), shared configuration (interest rate, tax rate), constants (public static final), and shared state that belongs to the class rather than any individual object. Avoid mutable static variables in multi-threaded applications — they are shared state and require synchronization. Access via ClassName.variableName — not via instance reference.

items.q: Q4. What is the default value of instance variables in Java?
items.a: Instance variables are automatically initialized by Java: byte, short, int, long → 0. float → 0.0f. double → 0.0. char → '\u0000' (null character). boolean → false. Any object reference (String, arrays, custom classes) → null. Static variables get the same defaults. Local variables do NOT get defaults — using an uninitialized local variable is a compile-time error. The null default for object fields is a common source of NullPointerException when developers forget to initialize fields in constructors.

items.q: Q5. What is the var keyword in Java? What are its limitations?
items.a: var (Java 10+) enables local variable type inference — the compiler infers the variable's type from the initializer expression. var name = 'Alice'; — inferred as String. var list = new ArrayList<String>(); — inferred as ArrayList<String>. var is still statically typed — type is fixed at compile time. Limitations: (1) Only for local variables — not fields, parameters, or return types. (2) Must have an initializer — var x; is invalid. (3) Cannot initialize to null — var x = null; is invalid (type cannot be inferred). (4) Cannot be used in lambda parameter types (var x -> x.length() — invalid). Use var when the type is obvious from context; avoid when it reduces readability.

items.q: Q6. What is a final variable in Java? What is the difference between final primitive and final reference?
items.a: A final variable can be assigned only once. Reassignment causes a compile error. For final primitive (final int x = 10;): the VALUE is constant — cannot be changed. For final reference (final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();): the REFERENCE is constant — cannot be reassigned to point to a different object. However, the object's internal state CAN be modified: list.add('item') is valid even if list is final. For a truly immutable object, the class itself must be immutable (like String). Constants are declared as public static final with UPPER_SNAKE_CASE names. Local final variables must be initialized before use. Instance final variables must be set in constructors.

items.q: Q7. Can a local variable and an instance variable have the same name? What happens?
items.a: Yes — a local variable can have the same name as an instance variable. The local variable shadows (hides) the instance variable within its scope. Inside the method, using the variable name refers to the local variable. To access the instance variable when shadowed, use this.variableName. Example: class has field int value = 100. Method declares int value = 200. Inside method: value = 200 (local), this.value = 100 (instance). This is intentionally used in constructors and setters: this.name = name; — parameter name shadows field name, this.name refers to the field. Java does NOT allow a local variable to shadow another local variable in the same method scope — that is a compile error.

items.q: Q8. What is variable scope in Java? Explain with examples.
items.a: Scope defines the region of code where a variable is accessible. Java has four scope levels: (1) Class scope: static variables — accessible throughout the class and (with qualifier) from outside. (2) Instance scope: instance variables — accessible throughout the class via this. (3) Method scope: local variables declared in method — accessible only within that method. (4) Block scope: variables declared inside a block (if, for, while, try) — accessible only within that block. Attempting to access a variable outside its scope is a compile error. Java uses block-based scoping (like C/C++), not function-based scoping (like JavaScript's var). The tighter the scope, the safer and more readable the code.

Output when show() is called: 30, 20, 10. x inside show(): 30 — local variable x shadows the static field x. The local variable takes precedence within the method scope. this.y: 20 — accesses the instance variable y (no shadowing here). Test.x: 10 — accesses the static field x via class name, bypassing the local variable shadow. This demonstrates: (1) local variables shadow static variables in the same scope, (2) ClassName.staticVar always refers to the class field regardless of shadowing, (3) this.instanceVar always refers to the instance field.

items.q: Q10. Why does int result = 7 / 2 give 3 and not 3.5?
items.a: In Java, when both operands of / are integers (int, long), the result is also an integer — the decimal part is truncated (not rounded). 7 / 2 = 3 (remainder 1 is discarded). This is integer division. To get a floating-point result, at least one operand must be a double or float. Fix options: (1) Cast one operand: double result = (double) 7 / 2; → 3.5. (2) Use double literals: double result = 7.0 / 2; → 3.5. (3) Store in double, use double operands: double a = 7, b = 2; double result = a / b; → 3.5. Common bug: double result = a / b; where a and b are int — division happens as int first, then the result (3) is widened to double 3.0, not 3.5.

blocks.text: Challenge yourself with these practice questions. Attempt each independently before reading the answer — active recall is proven to be 2–3x more effective than passive reading.

items.a: Does NOT compile. Error: 'variable a might not have been initialized'. Local variable a is declared but never assigned a value. Java does not give local variables default values — using an uninitialized local variable is a compile-time error (not a runtime error). Fix: int a = 0; or assign a before the expression int c = a + b;. Note: if a were an instance variable instead of local, it would default to 0 and compile fine.

Output: 1, 2, 3. count is a static variable — one shared copy. Each Counter() constructor increments the shared count and assigns the current value to the instance's id. After c1: count=1, c1.id=1. After c2: count=2, c2.id=2. After c3: count=3, c3.id=3. c1.id=1, c2.id=2, Counter.count=3. This demonstrates the classic use of static variables as shared counters — each instance gets a unique sequential ID from the shared counter.

Output: 100, 50. Inside display(), the local variable int x = 100 shadows the instance variable x = 50. Using x alone refers to the local variable (100). Using this.x explicitly refers to the instance variable (50). This is the classic variable shadowing pattern — most commonly seen in constructors: this.name = name where parameter shadows field. The this keyword is used to disambiguate between instance variable and local variable when they share a name.

Does NOT compile. Error: 'variable result might not have been initialized'. Although the if-block assigns result, the compiler cannot guarantee radius > 0 will always be true — so there is a code path (radius <= 0) where result is never assigned, and returning it would be unsafe. fix options — Option A (initialize with default): final double result; → change to double result = 0.0; remove final if needed. Option B (handle both branches): double result; if (radius > 0) { result = Math.PI * radius * radius; } else { result = 0.0; } return result;. Option C (direct return): return (radius > 0) ? Math.PI * radius * radius : 0.0; — cleanest.

Output: 2147483647, -2147483648, 2147483648. max = Integer.MAX_VALUE = 2147483647 (largest int value). max + 1: integer overflow — adding 1 to the maximum int value wraps around to the minimum int value (-2147483648) silently. No exception is thrown — Java does not check for integer overflow. (long) max + 1: the cast to long happens first (max becomes 2147483647L), then + 1 produces 2147483648L — correct result. If max + 1L were used, both operands would be long. Takeaway: always use long when values may exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE (~2.1 billion).

Variable types: department — instance variable (String, default null). companyName — static variable (String, initialized to 'Tech Corp'). salary — local variable (method parameter, always initialized). rate — local variable (declared but NEVER initialized — compile error!). bonus — local variable (uses uninitialized rate — also compile error). Issues: (1) rate is a local variable without initialization — using it in salary * rate causes compile error: 'variable rate might not have been initialized'. (2) department is an instance variable with default null — if used without null check, could cause NPE. Fix: double rate = 0.15; (or pass as parameter). Also consider initializing department in constructor.

Output: 30, Hello Java. sum = x + y = 10 + 20 = 30. final int means the value cannot be reassigned — x, y, sum are all constant after initialization. sb.append(' Java'): valid — final reference means sb cannot be reassigned to a different StringBuilder object, but the object itself is mutable. Calling methods that mutate the StringBuilder's content is perfectly legal. The commented line sb = new StringBuilder('New') would cause a compile error: 'cannot assign a value to final variable sb'. Key insight: final on an object reference locks the reference, not the object's internal state. For truly immutable objects, the class must be designed immutable (like String).

sections.title: Conclusion — Variables: The Foundation of Every Java Program

blocks.text: Variables are the most fundamental building block of any Java program — every computation, every piece of state, every result flows through them. Understanding the three types — local, instance, and static — and choosing the right one for each situation is a core Java skill. Local variables for temporary computation, instance variables for object state, static variables for class-wide shared data or constants.

Professional Java code treats variable design as a first-class concern: tight scope (declare where needed, not at the top), meaningful names (no magic numbers, no cryptic abbreviations), final where possible (signal immutability, prevent reassignment bugs), and correct types (long for large numbers, double for decimals, boolean with is/has prefix). These habits cost nothing at runtime but make code dramatically more readable, maintainable, and bug-resistant.

items.q: What are the types of variables in Java?
items.a: Java has three types of variables: (1) Local variables — inside methods/blocks, no default value, must initialize before use, stack-stored, block-scoped. (2) Instance variables — in class body outside methods, default values (0/false/null), heap-stored, one copy per object. (3) Static variables — with static keyword in class body, default values, method-area-stored, one copy shared by all instances, accessed via ClassName.varName.

items.q: What is the var keyword in Java?
items.a: var (Java 10+) is local variable type inference — the compiler infers the type from the right-hand side. var name = 'Alice'; is inferred as String. var is still statically typed — the type is fixed at compile time. Restrictions: local variables only (not fields/parameters/return types), must have an initializer, cannot be null. Use when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, especially for long generic types.

items.q: What is the difference between local, instance, and static variables in Java?
items.a: Local: method/block scope, no default value, stack-stored, one per method call. Instance: class scope, default values, heap-stored, one per object. Static: class-wide scope, default values, method-area-stored, one copy shared by all objects. Use local for temp computation, instance for object state, static for shared data or constants.

items.q: What are the naming conventions for variables in Java?
items.a: Variables use camelCase — start lowercase, capitalize each word: firstName, totalAmount, isActive. Constants (static final) use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MAX_SIZE, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT. Boolean variables use is/has/can prefix: isActive, hasPermission. Must start with letter, underscore, or $. Cannot be a Java keyword. Case-sensitive.

items.q: What is a final variable in Java?
items.a: A final variable can only be assigned once. For primitives, the value is constant. For object references, the reference is fixed but the object's state can still be mutated. Local final must be initialized before use. Instance final must be set in every constructor. Static final constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Reassigning a final variable is a compile-time error.
